name: Semiconductors
one_liner: Designers and manufacturers of chips, a cyclical, capital-intensive industry where process leadership and scale create steep barriers to entry.
how_it_makes_money: Chip designers sell processors, memory, and analog/power components to device makers, cloud providers, and automakers, either manufacturing themselves (integrated device makers) or outsourcing to foundries (fabless). Foundries charge per wafer, while equipment and IP vendors sell tools and license designs to the rest of the chain.
revenue_formula: Revenue = units shipped × average selling price (ASP)
Foundry revenue = wafers processed × price per wafer (driven by node)
Units per wafer = good dies per wafer × yield
cost_structure: Fab capex and depreciation: leading-edge fabs cost tens of billions and dominate costs for manufacturers
R&D: design and process development, often ~15-25% of revenue for leading firms
Materials and wafers: silicon, chemicals, gases, and photomasks
Equipment: lithography and deposition tools, with a few near-monopoly suppliers
Labor and energy for fab operations
margins: Leading fabless and foundry firms can earn gross margins of roughly 50-70%+, while memory makers swing between losses and high profits through the cycle. Process leadership, product differentiation, and capacity utilization drive the spread.

key_metrics.name: Gross margin
key_metrics.what: Captures pricing power and manufacturing efficiency; a key signal of differentiation.

key_metrics.name: Yield
key_metrics.what: Share of working chips per wafer; small improvements sharply lower unit cost.

key_metrics.name: Fab utilization
key_metrics.what: Share of manufacturing capacity in use; high fixed costs make it critical to profitability.

key_metrics.name: Process node (nm)
key_metrics.what: Generation of manufacturing technology; leadership determines performance and pricing power.

key_metrics.name: Book-to-bill ratio
key_metrics.what: Orders received versus units billed; an indicator of where the cycle is heading.

key_metrics.name: Inventory days
key_metrics.what: Chips held in inventory; rising levels often signal a coming downturn.

trends: AI accelerator demand concentrating profits in GPUs, high-bandwidth memory, and advanced packaging
Government subsidies and export controls reshaping where fabs are built and who can buy advanced chips
Onshoring of manufacturing to the US, Europe, and Japan to reduce reliance on Taiwan
Advanced packaging and chiplets becoming a key battleground as node shrinks slow
Hyperscalers designing their own custom chips
Uneven cycle: AI booming while consumer, auto, and industrial chip demand recovers more slowly

case_angles.question: Should a chipmaker build a new fab in the US given available subsidies?
